newsitem.title: FRANCE: French no comment on Alcatel's Thomson-CSF hopes.
newsitem.headline: French no comment on Alcatel's Thomson-CSF hopes.

text.p: The French government declined comment on Saturday on a report that it planned to cut its stake in defence electronics firm Thomson-CSF to 40 percent despite calling off its privatisation.

Le Figaro newspaper quoted sources close to Prime Minister Lionel Jospin on Saturday as saying he envisaged a role for private engineering giant Alcatel-Alsthom in Thomson-CSF, with the state retaining 40 percent and 20 percent in the hands of stock market investors.
A spokesman for Jospin said he could not comment on the report but added no decisions had been taken at this stage.
The Socialist-led government said on Friday it was scrapping a process launched by the previous centre-right government aimed at selling the state's 58 percent stake in Thomson-CSF.
It said it would propose within weeks an alternative plan to build a French conglomerate around the company, one of Europe's largest electronics manufacturers for the defence industry.
Alcatel had bid for Thomson-CSF in competition with missiles-to-publishing group Lagardere , which was teamed up with Daimler Benz Aerospace (DASA) .
Friday's statement made clear the government would keep significant control over Thomson-CSF with a "decisive" public stake, but left open exactly how big this share would be.
Afternoon daily Le Monde quoted DASA as saying it was awaiting an explanation from the French government before reacting.

Jospin's decision focused attention on the fragile French and European defence industries during a Bastille Day holiday weekend leading up to Monday's traditional parade of French weaponry marking the anniversary of the 1789 revolution.

Conservative President Jacques Chirac, who may talk about Thomson-CSF in a Bastille Day television interview on Monday, has said the company should be a national champion and play a key role in the restucturing of European defence firms.

Defence industry analysts said the new Socialist-led government's decision had left the French defence industry potentially isolated in Europe and meant it could face tough internal restructuring before moving forward with alliances.
It also meant France and Europe could lose more vital time in their race to team up to face tough competition from U.S. defence groups that have merged and increased their efficiency.
"One can see that the French industry is isolated," Natexis Capital analyst Antoine Nodet said. "Before this decision it (internal restructuring) was a choice, now it is an imperative."

Since French defence companies are too small to tackle the world market alone and virtually all the major European companies have already formed alliances, French firms must link up if they want to be major international players, he said.
